claims.claim: Node handles one thing at a time per process, so while a report rendered (~400 ms CPU), all other requests waited behind it
claims.why: Every server ran on a single CPU, and no test mixes long CPU-bound requests with short ones, so the benchmark cannot show head-of-line blocking or single-threaded behaviour.

claims.claim: Waiting on the queued job only waits on I/O, so the Express API keeps serving other requests (/tasks) meanwhile
claims.measured: I/O wait test (10 ms per request, 256 connections): node-express 14,188 req/s, p50 16.66 ms, p99 35.39 ms
claims.why: Express kept 256 requests waiting on I/O at once and still served about 14k req/s, so waiting on I/O did not stop it handling other requests.

claims.claim: Rendering is synchronous CPU work, so the worker runs one job at a time per process, and the way to go faster is more worker machines
claims.why: Only single-CPU containers were measured, so nothing shows how a Node process uses extra cores or how throughput grows with more processes.
